#7682. Pactiv Evergreen settles for $6.25M over 2023 North Carolina mill closure

The restitution amount is more than half of what Pactiv Evergreen received from the state in economic development grants for the site.

The paper mill in Canton had been in operation for more than 100 years prior to then-owner Pactiv shutting it down in 2023, according to the state of North Carolina. Blue Ridge Paper Products operated the facility since 1999, and in 2007 that company became Evergreen Packaging through a merger. Pactiv Evergreen formed in 2020 through the combination of Evergreen Packaging and Pactiv, both of which were previously acquired by Reynolds Group Holdings.

At the time of the Canton mill’s closure, many people expressed surprise at Pactiv Evergreen’s decision. The company made the announcement in March 2023 along with other closure and restructuring disclosures, and CEO Mike King noted a “challenging market environment” for Pactiv’s beverage merchandising business. North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper said in a statement last week that the Canton closure came as a “gut punch" to the local and state economies.

Upon introducing the lawsuit in May 2024, then-Attorney General Josh Stein noted that taxpayers “invested in Pactiv Evergreen to bolster our state’s economy,” but Pactiv didn’t hold up its end of the bargain. He said at the time that his office had tried working with Pactiv for a year to address the company’s obligations, but it had “become clear that legal action was necessary to hold Pactiv accountable.” The initial lawsuit sought repayment of the full $12 million in economic incentives that Pactiv had received.

The settlement should not be viewed as an admission to wrongdoing, according to the North Carolina Department of Justice.

“Pactiv broke its promise to the state and the people of Canton, and today’s settlement holds it accountable for violating its agreement,” Attorney General Jeff Jackson, who was elected in November and took office last month, said of the new settlement. “This settlement will allow the people of Canton and Haywood County to immediately put millions back into rebuilding their economy after the mill’s closure, and it will shield them from future litigation from Pactiv.”

The candidates for state attorney general repeatedly brought up the mill issues on the campaign trail prior to November’s election. Both candidates expressed a desire to hold Pactiv accountable.

Pactiv had filed a motion to dismiss the complaint in July 2024. But a judge denied that motion in October, allowing the lawsuit to proceed.

“We are pleased to have resolved with the State of North Carolina all outstanding matters relating to the closure and sale of our former Canton mill site. We thank our employees for their contributions to our company and wish the Canton community well in this next chapter for the Town,” said Pactiv Evergreen Tuesday in an emailed statement.

This wasn’t Pactiv’s first legal battle over the Canton site.

In autumn 2023, the company reached a settlement worth more than $2 million with the U.S. EPA over Clean Air Act violations at Canton. Earlier that year, the North Carolina Department of Environmental Quality said the site violated water quality requirements; the company denied the allegations. In 2021 and 2022, the mill faced state air quality violations.

Novolex is in the process of acquiring Pactiv Evergreen for $6.7 billion. The deal, which would take Pactiv private, is expected to close during the first half of this year.

#7681. Whose tradition, which history? Agency adjudication and Sun Valley Orchards

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

Over the past few decades, several features of the administrative state have been subject to heated constitutional challenge. One of them is agency adjudication: the practice of resolving disputes “in-house” within administrative agencies instead of addressing these disputes directly in a court. Of late, the Supreme Court has applied a “history-and-tradition” methodology to assess the constitutionality of agency adjudication. But that methodology confronts the challenge of how to select from among multiple competing traditions the one that should carry the day. On Nov. 10, the court will hear a case, Department of Labor v. Sun Valley Orchards, that underscores the difficulties of carrying out its history-and-tradition methodology – difficulties that apply across many areas of law.

By way of background, the basic constitutional issue regarding administrative adjudication is as follows. Article III of the Constitution vests the “judicial power of the United States” in the Supreme Court and lower federal courts. From the founding and onward, however, disputes that fall within the jurisdiction of Article III courts have been heard in tribunals belonging to the other federal branches, such as territorial courts, military tribunals, bankruptcy courts, magistrate judges, and most pertinent for current purposes, administrative tribunals – for instance, by administrative law judges.

Agency adjudication of, say, Social Security and veterans’ benefits claims is an integral part of the administrative state. It provides a streamlined way of handling these claims and avoids clogging up the Article III courts. Although there is usually a right to appeal administrative determinations at some point to Article III courts, these courts apply a deferential standard of review.

The question arises whether administrative adjudication is compatible with the judicial scheme laid out in Article III of the Constitution. This is a practically significant issue; agency dispute resolution has substantial effects on individuals and companies, who can face considerable fines or penalties. To what extent, then, is agency adjudication outside Article III courts justified? And what kinds of limitations should be placed on it?

In the past few decades, the Supreme Court has turned to “history and tradition” to answer these questions. History and tradition as methods of constitutional interpretation are likely most familiar from cases on hot-button social issues, such as Dobbs (holding that there was no “history and tradition” of a right to have an abortion) and Bruen (holding that there was no “history and tradition” of requiring certain types of licenses to carry firearms outside the home). But the court has also drawn on history and tradition to shape the scope of federal judicial power, in contexts ranging from Article III standing to equitable remedies. One such setting is the division of labor between Article III courts and agency adjudicative bodies.

History and tradition play a dual role in the law of adjudication outside Article III courts. This pattern was on display in the Supreme Court’s 2024 case Securities and Exchange Commission v. Jarkesy, which addressed the constitutionality of agency adjudication of certain claims involving securities fraud. First, tradition provides a justification for non-Article III (including agency) adjudication of a limited class of claims deemed to involve “public rights,” that is, matters which historically “could have been determined exclusively by [the executive and legislative] branches.” In Jarkesy, the court listed “the collection of revenue,” “immigration,” “tariffs,” “relations with Indian tribes,” “the administration of public lands,” and “the granting of public benefits such as payments to veterans, pensions, and patent rights” as members of this class of claims. Since these matters, the court explained, historically could have been adjudicated outside Article III courts, they may be heard by non-Article III tribunals today.

Second, tradition provides a reason that claims involving “private” rather than “public” rights must be brought before Article III courts instead of administrative tribunals. A hallmark of a private-rights suit that belongs before an Article III court, the Jarkesy court stated, is being “made of the stuff of the traditional actions at common law tried by the courts at Westminster in 1789.”

In Jarkesy, the court decided that the securities fraud claim at issue resembled common-law fraud, a traditional common-law claim and so a private right requiring an Article III tribunal. (The court also emphasized that the remedy the SEC was pursuing – civil penalties – was historically enforceable in courts of law; accordingly, the SEC was bringing a suit “at common law” to which the Seventh Amendment jury trial right attached. Jarkesy thus revolved substantially around the jury trial right, which is not a question directly presented in Sun Valley.)

Tradition, then, helps to demarcate the boundary between claims that must be adjudicated by Article III courts (private rights) and claims that may be resolved before other courts, including administrative agencies (public rights). But how should the court decide whether a present-day claim fits into a tradition of private rights or public rights? In particular, what should the court do when there are multiple traditions into which a present-day claim might fit?

The court’s upcoming case Sun Valley provides an example of the problem of “too many traditions.” Sun Valley involves a nonimmigrant visa program, administered jointly by the Department of Labor and the Department of Homeland Security, that permits American employers to hire foreign laborers to perform temporary or seasonal agricultural work. As a condition of participating in the program, employers agree to provide certain workplace arrangements to both foreign and domestic workers. DOL found that Sun Valley, a New Jersey farm, had failed to provide these arrangements, and the agency assessed hundreds of thousands of dollars in civil penalties and back wages against Sun Valley. Sun Valley was required to contest these penalties before an administrative law judge, with deferential review by an Article III court. Sun Valley challenged the administrative-adjudication requirement as a violation of Article III, and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 3rd Circuit agreed with Sun Valley.

In Supreme Court briefing, the government and Sun Valley both appeal to the history-and-tradition methodology of Jarkesy, but they sharply disagree about which tradition is relevant. The government emphasizes traditions related to immigration. According to the government, its enforcement action fits within two historical categories of public rights adjudication that did not require Article III courts: rights “belonging to the sovereign, such as the right to determine whether to allow aliens into the country,” and “privileges conferred by the government, such as public benefits granted under government programs.” In the government’s view, Sun Valley violated the conditions of bringing foreign workers to the United States through an immigration program that offered the farm a benefit. The pertinent tradition is hence the history of adjudicating immigration- and benefits- related claims outside Article III courts.

Sun Valley, by contrast, casts its claim as akin to common-law breach of contract – a traditional private right requiring an Article III tribunal. DOL’s allegation, Sun Valley observes, was that Sun Valley had violated its agreement to provide certain working conditions to foreign and domestic workers. That allegation, Sun Valley contends, is simply a charge that Sun Valley breached a contract. Sun Valley further argues that DOL sought common-law remedies and in particular civil penalties – more evidence that the claim at issue involves a private right. To Sun Valley, the case is located outside the historical tradition of immigration adjudication because it is based on conditions of employment rather than immigration status. Consequently, it was unconstitutional for DOL to adjudicate Sun Valley’s dispute in-house.

Which party is right about the tradition into which the dispute over Sun Valley’s working conditions falls? Plausibly, the answer is “both.” Yes, the government is alleging that Sun Valley violated an agreement; but the agreement in question was concluded as part of an immigration program allowing Sun Valley to hire foreign workers.

So what are courts to do when, as here, they are faced with “too many traditions” – that is, traditions with different implications for the constitutional question at hand?

One possible response is to conclude that history-and-tradition analysis is hopelessly indeterminate and to reject this methodology. While many methods of constitutional interpretation fail to yield a single right answer, “history and tradition” is often justified precisely by its promise to produce constraint and fixity. Breaking this promise might be viewed as grounds for abandoning the history-and-tradition approach.

Complete repudiation of history and tradition, however, would be unwarranted. Historical practice has played an important role in both upholding and limiting non-Article III adjudication; it is a tool in judges’ toolbox and should not be thrown away.

Another option is to supplement history-and-tradition methodology, when it does not produce a clear result, with other modes of constitutional analysis. Earlier cases on non-Article III adjudication, for instance, appealed openly to practical considerations of government efficiency.

A third option would be to draw on other “modalities” of constitutional interpretation to inform the choice of which strand of tradition to emphasize. One such modality is precedent. Jarkesy did not directly confront a program like the DOL’s in Sun Valley, so it is not controlling precedent. But Jarkesy did seem to treat Congress’ broad power over immigration as a reason to uphold agency adjudication in immigration-related cases. Perhaps this suggests that DOL’s enforcement action fits better into a traditional public-rights than private-rights category.

The court may also decide to avoid the problem of too many traditions by taking a statutory “out.” When it took the case, the court added a question regarding DOL’s statutory authority to impose civil penalties and back wages on Sun Valley. The court may decide that DOL lacks such statutory authority, potentially by appealing to constitutional avoidance (in other words, construing the statute to grant DOL such authority would raise serious questions about the constitutionality of agency adjudication, which should be avoided unless necessary to decide). But the statutory question is not straightforward, and resolving it may well have ramifications for a wide array of agency-imposed penalties. At any rate, one or more of the justices can be expected to opine on Article III in Sun Valley, and the Article III issue is bound to recur.

Overall, the problem of “too many traditions” is by no means unique to the context of non-Article III adjudication. The Supreme Court faces challenging questions about how to apply history-and-tradition methodology when a present-day practice could plausibly fit into multiple traditions. The court’s response to these questions may have an important impact not only on the future of agency adjudication, but also on the trajectory of historically driven interpretation across a variety of pressing constitutional debates.

Rachel Bayefsky is Professor of Law at the University of Virginia School of Law, where she writes about civil procedure, constitutional law, and legal theory. She clerked for Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg in the 2018-2019 Term.

#7680. What businesses should know about consent rules when calling consumers

Rules around obtaining consumer consent before calling or texting are in a state of legal and regulatory uncertainty – and companies should remain cautious.

Senosiain is an associate and Rollins is a shareholder at Gunster. Views are the authors’ own.

The Telephone Consumer Protection Act governs calls and text messages sent by businesses to consumers. One such rule is that businesses must obtain express written consent prior to sending text messages to consumers, if they are using an automated telephone dialing system or making calls using an artificial or pre-recorded voice, including the use of AI bots.

The TCPA also provides that businesses may not call or text consumers on the federal Do Not Call List unless prior express consent is given. Even basic telemarketing calls and text messages require prior express consent. Violation of the statute can trigger liability for up to $1,500 per call or text message sent.

Additionally, many states have their own version of the TCPA, deemed “mini-TCPAs,” that require compliance for all businesses who make calls to consumer-residents in that state, regardless of where the business is domiciled.

Many companies use lead generators which gather consumer consents for multiple businesses and then provide the companies with consent and contact information for those potential consumers. Lead generators who obtain proper written consent can be a very useful tool for companies. This was generally permissible under the TCPA.

However, in 2023, the Federal Communications Commission updated its TCPA rules requiring “one-to-one consent” which was to become effective Jan. 27, 2025.

The one-to-one consent rule provides that if a business uses an ATDS, artificial or prerecorded voice, the business must obtain prior express consent, one seller at a time.

Thus, it prevents lead generators from using a single consumer’s consent for multiple businesses. Additionally, the one-to-one consent rule provides that the consent must be clear and conspicuous, and the calls and texts initiated pursuant to the consent must be logically and topically associated with the interaction that prompted the consent. This rule applies to both text messages and phone calls.

On Jan. 24, 2025, the FCC postponed the 2023 order by a year, until Jan. 26, 2026. Later that same day the Eleventh Circuit Court of Appeals vacated the 2023 Order, thus eliminating the one-to-one consent rule.

The Eleventh Circuit Court of Appeals held “that the FCC exceeded its statutory authority under the TCPA because the 2023 Order’s new consent restrictions impermissibly conflict[ed] with the ordinary statutory meaning of prior express consent.”

Notably, the court ruled that the FCC exceeded its statutory authority at the outset, when it created the one-to-one consent rule. The court held that the 2023 Order’s one-to-one prior express consent restriction impermissibly conflicted with the ordinary statutory meaning of “prior express consent.” Thus, the Court vacated application of the 2023 Order, and remanded for further proceedings.

As a result, it is very likely that we will see other cases challenging TCPA regulations, especially as to the consent required before making a telemarketing call or text message using an ATDS.

It is unclear whether the FCC will revise its 2023 Order to comply with the Eleventh Circuit’s decision. In order to be prepared for this rule to come into effect, and in an abundance of caution, businesses who use lead generators to source potential consumers’ consent should ascertain that the lead generators are obtaining individual, one-to-one consent.

Businesses should also only contact consumers who provide this consent for telemarketing that is logically and topically associated with that which the consent was provided. Further, in addition to storing consumer contact information, businesses must retain the consent forms, information as to when consent was given, and through whom. Even businesses that do not use lead generators to obtain consent should continue to review their consent practices to ensure strict compliance with the TCPA and mini-TCPAs.

The TCPA requires prior express consent, and in many cases, prior express written consent, for calls and text messages made to prospective consumers. Regardless of any changes to the TCPA, the FTSA still requires that businesses obtain prior express written consent when making unsolicited telephone calls (including sending text messages) using an automated system. And lastly, to further protect your business, the consent form should have robust terms of service, including a class action waiver.

We continue to recommend that businesses ensure compliance with the TCPA, FTSA, and any other state regulations by always obtaining express written consent prior to contacting potential consumers via calls or text messages.

#7679. Court declines to hear dispute tied to George Floyd protests and cases involving former baseball player Roberto Clemente and actor Randy Quaid

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

The Supreme Court on Monday denied review in over 200 cases, including a dispute that arose in Minneapolis after the murder of George Floyd in police custody in 2020 and clashes involving actor Randy Quaid and the sons of a baseball legend. These denials were part of a list of orders from the court’s Nov. 6 conference that was released on Monday morning.

The court on Friday granted one petition for review from that conference, in a case involving whether and when a bankruptcy court can refuse to honor an agreement to arbitrate disputes.

The Minneapolis case was brought by a group of businesses located at the intersection where Floyd was killed. Following Floyd’s death, the city blocked the intersection “with concrete barricades,” which “prevented vehicles and pedestrians from accessing” the area, and withdrew police protection, according to the businesses’ petition for review. Those barricades remained in place “for over one year,” and led to significant economic losses for the businesses and a surge in violent crime, the petition said.

The businesses challenged the city’s actions in state court, alleging that it had violated the Constitution’s takings clause and similar protections in Minnesota’s constitution by interfering with their operations and failing to compensate them accordingly. However, a district court and the Minnesota Court of Appeals disagreed, and the Minnesota Supreme Court denied the businesses’ request for it to review the case.

In August, the businesses came to the Supreme Court, asking the justices to revive their case. On Monday, the Supreme Court declined to do so without comment.

The case involving family members of baseball legend Roberto Clemente also involved the takings clause. Clemente’s adult sons and companies associated with preserving Clemente’s legacy challenged Puerto Rico’s use of the baseball legend’s image on “license plates and tags,” an initiative that “generat[ed] 15 million dollars for Puerto Rico” but also fueled ill will against the family, “who Puerto Ricans thought were to blame for a fee levied on them during dire economic times,” according to the petition for review. Through their lawsuit, the Clementes aimed to block Puerto Rico from using their father’s image in the future and recover financial damages.

Earlier this year, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 1st Circuit prevented the Clemente family’s takings clause claim from proceeding, emphasizing that it (along with the federal statute concerning trademark law) is “designed not to protect legacies but instead to remedy ... the taking of property for public use without just compensation.” In June, the Clementes asked the Supreme Court to take up the case and, among other things, clarify that the takings clause can apply in cases involving intangible property.

After considering the petition at three consecutive conferences, the justices on Monday denied review.

In Monday’s order list, the justices also asked the United States solicitor general to share the government’s views on AstraZeneca UK Ltd. v. Atchley, a case on whether U.S. terrorism victims may sue 21 “of the world’s largest pharmaceutical and medical-device companies” under the Antiterrorism Act for allegedly aiding and abetting terrorists in Iraq.

Additionally, the justices sent Roybal v. Griffith, a transgender female inmate’s challenge to jail policies in El Paso County, Colorado, regarding the treatment of transgender inmates back to the lower court for reconsideration in light of West Virginia v. B.P.J. and United States v. Skrmetti.

In B.P.J., the court ruled in June that state laws barring transgender female athletes from participating on women’s and girls’ sports teams do not violate a federal civil rights law or the equal protection clause of the 14th Amendment. In Skrmetti, the court last year upheld a Tennessee law prohibiting some medical treatments for transgender minors, holding that it was not subject to heightened scrutiny under the equal protection clause.

Also on Monday, the justices granted the solicitor general’s request to participate in three oral arguments during the December argument session:

Kelsey Dallas is SCOTUSblog's managing editor and the primary author of the SCOTUStoday newsletter.

Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

#7677. Judge removed for engaging in ‘extensive and severe misconduct’

A Los Angeles County Superior Court judge has been removed from his position for making inappropriate racial and sexual comments and several other instances of misconduct. (Photo from Shutterstock)

A Los Angeles County Superior Court judge has been removed from his position for making inappropriate racial and sexual comments and several other instances of misconduct.

In its decision Tuesday, the California Commission on Judicial Performance said Los Angeles County Superior Court Judge Robert Draper “persistently violated the standards governing judicial behavior and engaged in extensive and severe misconduct.” The commission also said the judge failed to accept responsibility or show remorse for his actions.

Among the charges, the commission considered Draper’s conduct during a February 2023 posttrial hearing in a sexual harassment case, where he lectured a Black attorney about Black football players and race relations in the South. It also examined comments that Draper made to female attorneys in the case—while in his chambers—about male attorneys who slept with their secretaries at his prior law firm.

Other charges alleged that Draper made inappropriate comments to a female colleague and a female court personnel, engaged in improper ex parte communications, and improperly disclosed confidential juvenile records.

Draper has said the charges “were contrary to all credible evidence and/or taken wholly out of context.”

An attorney who represented Draper didn’t respond to a request for comment from Courthouse News Service.

SEATTLE (CN) â A mother who was struck by a bullet while dining with her daughters at a Cheesecake Factory in Washington state failed to convince a federal judge that the restaurant and the mallâs security company were liable.

Larisa Sopka and her daughters were dining at the Cheesecake Factory at Westfield Southcenter Mall in Tukwila in May 2022 when chaos erupted in the restaurant. Nearby patrons in the midst of an argument fired a gun, and the bullet struck Sopkaâs left leg.

But on Tuesday, U.S. District Judge Barbara Rothstein found the Cheesecake Factory could not have reasonably anticipated the shooting and dismissed the plaintiffsâ negligence claims.

âRowdy table behavior at The Cheesecake Factory had never in the past led to gun violence of any kind, and it was not reasonable for the staff to have anticipated that gunshots would be fired in the restaurant on the evening of May 31, 2022 in sufficient time to have prevented it or provided any earlier warning than the shout of âgunâ that occurred that night,â Rothstein, a the Jimmy Carter appointee, wrote.

In January 2024, Sopka and her daughters first sued the mall and the Cheesecake Factory in January 2024, accusing both of failing to safeguard the premises despite ârampant crime and violence.â In an amended complaint, the plaintiffs added the mallâs security contractor, Allied Universal Security Services, as a defendant.

But Rothstein also dismissed the claims against the security company. Under its contract with the mall, Allied Universal patrols the premise of the mall, but employees were told not to go into a tenant space unless specifically requested.

The shooting occurred inside the restaurant and the security company didnât have a contractual duty to monitor or patrol inside the Cheesecake Factory.

âThe evidence does not support a finding that Allied had any control over security for the restaurant that would create a duty to protect the plaintiffs in the restaurant from a criminal act, even if it were foreseeable,â Rothstein wrote.

There was evidence before the court of âunruly and loud behaviorâ inside the restaurant, but Rothstein found it insufficient to establish that gunfire was imminent.

âThere is no evidence that Allied assumed responsibility for the safety of The Cheesecake Factory customers, there is no evidence that Allied knew or should have known of the specific threat, even though it may have been aware of car thefts or other violent incidents that had occurred at Southcenter Mall in the past, and there is no evidence that Allied failed to respond to a call for assistance,â Rothstein wrote.

The Sopka family had claimed the mall was the site of âscores of crimes, including assaults, shootings, carjackings, robberies, thefts, and instances of domestic violenceâ since well before the May 2022 incident.

The plaintiffs contended the restaurant, security company and mall all failed to implement appropriate security protocols, noting one of the Cheesecake Factoryâs employees who worked at the location of the shooting told local news that âliterally anyone can walk in and shoot a gun. We donât have security or someone guarding the door.â

None of the parties responded to a request for comment before press time.

#7675. Supreme Court allows Trump administration to continue border wall construction

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

The Supreme Court on Monday cleared the way for the Trump administration to resume construction of a border wall in the Big Bend region of southwestern Texas. In a four-page, unsigned opinion, the justices granted the government’s request to pause an order by a federal district judge that had temporarily halted the project. Only Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson indicated, without explanation, that she would have denied the government’s request.

The dispute began earlier this year, when then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem and her successor, Markwayne Mullin, issued three waivers of various environmental and conservation laws to authorize construction of the wall in the Big Bend region, which includes parts of Big Bend National Park. Noem and Mullin relied on a provision of the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996 that gives the DHS secretary the power to “waive all legal requirements” necessary “to ensure expeditious construction” of border walls and roads. When they announced the waivers, Noem and Mullin indicated that the Big Bend area “is an area of high illegal entry” requiring additional walls and barriers.

A group of plaintiffs opposed to the construction – an environmental group, a local landowner who works as a river guide, and a group formed to preserve a church – went to federal court to challenge the waivers’ legality. On Oct. 2, U.S. District Judge Kathleen Cardone temporarily barred the Department of Homeland Security from continuing construction on the border wall in the Big Bend region “until and unless” the government complies with environmental and other applicable laws.

In a written opinion that she released on Oct. 14, Cardone reasoned that the challengers were likely to prevail on their claim that the DHS secretary did not have the authority to issue the waivers. She relied on the major questions doctrine – the idea that if Congress intends to give a federal agency the power to make decisions of vast economic or political significance, it must say so very clearly. In particular, she emphasized, the Big Bend region is not an area with a high number of illegal entries. To the contrary, she stated, although it “comprises over 25% of the U.S.-Mexico border,” it makes up only a tiny percentage (“between 0.3% and 2.2%”) of the migrants apprehended while crossing the border. Therefore, she wrote, “if the Big Bend Sector is an area of high illegal entry, so is every other sector, and the waiver authority would apply to the entire U.S.-Mexico border. If that were the case, Congress could have simply authorized construction ‘to deter illegal crossings.’” The major questions doctrine instructs courts to avoid “interpretations that would render limiting language meaningless,” Cardone concluded.

After Cardone declined to pause her ruling to give the government time to seek Supreme Court review, the Trump administration came to the Supreme Court, where it asked the justices not only to temporarily freeze Cardone’s order but also to grant review and summarily (that is, without additional briefing or oral argument) reverse it. U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer argued that Cardone lacked the power to consider the challengers’ claim based on the major questions doctrine because their complaint specifically alleged that the DHS secretary “lacked ‘clear congressional authorization’ … to issue the waivers” under the IIRIRA – which, he said, was a statutory claim that “Congress denied district courts” the authority “to entertain.” But in any event, Sauer continued, even if the DHS secretary’s power to issue waivers under IIRIRA “implicates a question of ‘vast economic and political significance,’ Congress did clearly authorize the Secretary both to build border barriers and to waive legal requirements in order to facilitate their expeditious construction.”

The challengers urged the justices to leave Cardone’s order in place. Eric Glitzenstein, a lawyer representing the plaintiffs, told the justices in a 40-page filing that if her order were paused or lifted, it would permit the Trump administration to “immediately resume blasting, bulldozing, road construction, and other border barrier-related construction across one of the most remote and ecologically and culturally significant landscapes in the United States.”

The challengers argued that the major questions doctrine applied to their claim. They emphasized that the DHS secretary’s “decision to waive myriad federal, state, local, and tribal laws across vast geography for the purpose of building border infrastructure, even through national and state parks where border crossings are miniscule, is a truly ‘extraordinary’ assertion of power.” Because Congress “did not clearly authorize the sweeping exercise of power asserted here,” they wrote, the government’s “actions therefore amount to a constitutional violation of the major questions doctrine.”

In Monday’s opinion, the justices denied the government’s request to summarily reverse Cardone’s ruling but granted its request to put it on hold. “The Government,” the court explained, “is exceedingly likely to prevail on its argument” that Cardone did not have the power to consider the challengers’ “so-called major-questions-doctrine claim.” That claim, the court emphasized, contends only “that the Secretary exceeded his statutory authority,” which is not a constitutional claim. This is true, the court continued, even if the challengers rely on the major-questions doctrine, because that doctrine is a rule used to interpret laws. “There is no such thing as a ‘constitutional’ major-questions claim.”

The other factors that courts normally consider in deciding whether to pause a lower court’s decision also point in the government’s favor, the justices said. For example, Cardone’s order “delays the Government’s construction of border barriers and roads in the Big Bend Sector” and, as a result, “impedes the Government from advancing its ‘compelling interests’ in border security and integrity.” Moreover, the government is suffering permanent harm from the costs – “nearly half a million dollars … per day” – that it is incurring while the construction is on hold, but which cannot be recovered. Finally, the court wrote, “[t]he Government’s interest … outweighs any aesthetic, recreational, and environmental harm alleged by” the challengers.

Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

In his suit filed in Las Vegas District Court Tuesday, JesÃºs Antonio Rivas-Molina, a biology professor, claims disciplinary actions the university took against him violated his free speech and equal protection rights. He is asking the court to prohibit the university from enforcing or maintaining those sanctions, which include two written reprimands, removal from his position as department chair, a performance-improvement plan and a last-chance agreement.

The slew of disciplinary measures came after Rivas-Molina sent a message recommending a DEI initiative to all faculty and administration on March 27, 2025.

âIn this day and age where diversity principles are being attacked ferociously at the federal level, with so many universities caving and complying with the elimination of DEI initiatives, it is important that we double down in our commitment to promoting and supporting diversity in our university,â Rivas-Molina wrote in the message.

After faculty members claimed Rivas-Molina’s proposal was âheteronormative, misogynistic, racist and unfairly biased," acting Provost Brandon Kempner launched an investigation into him, he says in his complaint.

When Rivas-Molina learned of the external investigation in April 2025, he sent an email to a faculty association, stating he believed the accusations were retaliatory and complaining that the faculty senate, faculty association and the university were âmarching at locked step with the federal government.â Rivas-Molina later compared the criticisms of him to language white supremacist groups use when talking about DEI being racist against white people.

Despite university policy requiring otherwise, the school did not interview witnesses Rivas-Molina identified during the external investigation, he says in his complaint. He says he continued to push back, approaching Kempner and other university officials in August 2025 and arguing the âenforcement of different treatment against him for handbook violations was discriminatory." He claims officials then threatened to block him from using his university email.

Put on probation, Rivas-Molina says the university ordered him to file a monthly report on his progress toward being “more inclusive in his communications.” He says he was eventually threatened with termination, and that the university rejected a recommendation from a New Mexico Public Employee Labor Relations Board hearing officer to rescind the initial disciplinary actions taken against him.

The biology professor, who identifies as Hispanic and is from Venezuela, claims the university discriminated against other professors as well, saying that a professor from India left the university after it failed to investigate racist comments made by another faculty member.

The defendants include NMHUâs Board of Regents, Kempner, Kathy Jenkins, Jennifer Lindline, Brown, Lekan, Josh Hanna, Neil Woolf and 10 unnamed defendants. The case is assigned to Chief Judge Flora Gallegos, and Rivas, who is represented by attorney Eric Sirotkin, requested a 12-person jury for trial.

The parties did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

#7672. A blue ripple in Idaho raises questions about its political future

Democrats flipped six legislative seats this year, potentially giving them more influence over state budget decisions.

BOISE, Idaho (CN) â While a blue tsunami hit several states in the nation during midterm elections last week, decimating many Republican strongholds, Democrats’ impact in deep-red Idaho was more of a splash.

While Democrats swept every statewide office in Texas and Georgia, and made significant gains in other typically red and battleground states, their success in Idaho, where no Democrat has won a statewide office since 2002, was more modest: They gained six seats in the Idaho Legislature.

Nevertheless, those results got folks wondering: Could Idaho turn blue?

“Even though it didn’t result in a blue wave in Idaho, it certainly resulted in quite a few wavelets,” Ross Burkhart, a political science professor at Boise State University, said of the recent midterm election. “And those are actually fairly noticeable.”

Democrats flipped five state House seats and one state Senate seat, taking full control of three competitive districts in west Boise, the Magic Valley and Pocatello. Republicans still hold supermajorities in both chambers.

Burkhart said those districts have elected Democrats before, so the locations of the victories weren’t particularly surprising. What stood out to him was that all six seats flipped during the same election.

Markie McBrayer, an associate professor of political science at the University of Idaho, also said Idaho’s Democratic gains were more substantial than they might appear.

“Right now the narrative seems to be that Democrats didn’t make gains in Idaho or that the blue wave missed Idaho, but that’s not quite true,” McBrayer said.

Compared with the 2022 midterms, Idaho’s U.S. House races saw an average shift of about 12 percentage points toward Democrats, she said. The national shift was roughly 14 to 15 points.

But in Idaho, Republicans had much larger leads to begin with. In the 2022 and 2024 elections, Representative Russ Fulcher won by about 45 percentage points, while Representative Mike Simpson’s winning margins ranged from 25 to 30 points.

“These are numbers that are difficult to overcome with a wave,” McBrayer said.

She also said Idaho can’t be directly compared to states like Texas â where Democrats won a U.S. Senate seat for the first time since 1988 and the governor’s office for the first time since 1990 â and Georgia â which also elected its first Democratic governor in more than two decades â because of some key differences between them.

“Many of the comparisons being made right now are to states in the South,” she said. “These states are much more racially diverse and have a more traditionalistic political culture.”

Texas Democrats had also spent years trying to make the state competitive, she said, coming close in the 2018 U.S. Senate race.

Idaho, meanwhile, has a Republican voter registration advantage that Burkhart estimated at roughly six to one.

“There are more registered independents in Idaho than there are registered Democrats,” he said.

Still, not everyone who votes Republican thinks Idaho will stay that way.

Mike Owens, a Boise voter who asked to use an alias, described himself as a straight-ticket Republican, said he was surprised by the Democratic victories nationally. He blamed the results partly on inflation, the economy and war.

“I think gas prices and increased inflation prices across the board is number one,” Owens said. “I think the war is number two.”

His friend Steve Lewis, who described himself as fiscally conservative but somewhat more liberal on social issues, wasn’t as surprised. He said the economy likely played a role and pointed to the historical tendency for the president’s party to lose ground in midterm elections.

“I guess in hindsight, it was probably to be expected what happened, and I’m not overly concerned,” Lewis said.

But when asked whether Idaho could eventually turn blue, Owens said he thought it was possible.

“The influx of people is going to change that, and I think that there’s enough money getting thrown around in this state now to win elections to move the needle,” he said.

However, Burkhart said newcomers tend to be as conservative as longtime Idaho residents, particularly those settling in the northern and southwestern parts of the state.

“The people who’ve moved to Idaho are generally as conservative as people are in Idaho,” he said. “So they talk about partisan sorting, where you sort out based upon political persuasions â Idaho certainly has a reputation for being friendly for people on the right.”

According to Boise State University’s annual Idaho Public Policy Survey, about 40% of people who moved to Idaho in the past decade identified as Republicans, roughly the same proportion as long-term residents.

Despite being one of the most Republican states in the country, Idaho hasn’t always been so firmly red.

The state last voted for a Democratic presidential candidate in 1964, when Lyndon B. Johnson defeated Barry Goldwater. Democrats continued to hold prominent offices for decades afterward. Cecil Andrus served four terms as governor, leaving office in 1995. Frank Church represented Idaho in the U.S. Senate until 1981, and the state Senate was evenly divided between Democrats and Republicans as recently as 1990.

Burkhart said much of Idaho’s Democratic history was tied to labor unions in the timber, mining and railroad industries. Pocatello, a longtime Union Pacific railroad hub, developed a stronger Democratic tradition than many other Idaho cities. As those industries declined, so did the political influence of organized labor. The election of Ronald Reagan in 1980 also helped strengthen Republicans in Idaho, according to the professor.

“Some of the reasons for a strong Democratic Party began to disappear in Idaho, and weren’t really replaced by anything,” he said. “There was always a strong Republican presence too, but that resonated and remained afterwards.”

For some Democratic voters in Boise, the national election results brought relief, even if Idaho’s results were disappointing.

Alyssa Grimwis, Logan Hawk and Rosalind Triplett all said they voted primarily for Democrats. All three also supported Proposition 1, a ballot initiative that would have restored abortion rights in Idaho. Grimwis said she wanted to protect women’s rights and bring more balance to government. She voted for Democratic legislative candidates, “just hopefully to try to even things out a little bit more to get all voices heard.”

Hawk said she wasn’t surprised Idaho remained Republican, but the national results gave her some hope.

“I heard the news of the blue wave. I got up. My chest felt lighter. Like my steps were floating,” she said.

Triplett was particularly disappointed that Idaho voters rejected Proposition 1.

“Our low standard was at least Prop One would be yes, and they couldn’t even get that,â she said. “I feel like a lot of people find safety in being the âred Idaho.'”

The measure failed, with nearly 56% voting against it and 44% in favor. Burkhart said the margin was notable in a state where Republicans so heavily outnumber Democrats. He compared it with the defeat of a 2024 ballot initiative to introduce ranked-choice voting, which lost by roughly a two-to-one margin.

“The fact that that proposition was relatively close, I think, says something,” he said.

He said the results suggested more Democrats may have turned out to vote this year than in previous elections. But similar gains have happened before. Idaho Democrats picked up six legislative seats in 2006 and four in 2018, both years when Republicans faced political backlash.

Without a doubt, winning elections in Idaho remains an uphill battle for Democrats. McBrayer said some candidates have experimented with running as independents because Democrats have struggled to win more than 40% of the vote. One such example is Todd Achilles, a former Democratic state lawmaker who ran as an independent against Republican U.S. Senator Jim Risch this year. Achilles received about 33.5% of the vote.

Burkhart said Idaho Republicans have also benefited from decades of electoral success. He compared the party to a sports team with a winning tradition â one that can survive a difficult season.

“A strong political party combined with strong partisan registrations can withstand it,” he said.

For Democrats, however, the state’s six new legislative wins could still make a difference.

Burkhart said the gains might give the party more representation on legislative committees, including a possible additional seat on the Joint Finance-Appropriations Committee, which helps write Idaho’s budget. That could give Democrats a greater voice in budget decisions after lawmakers approved widespread spending cuts this year to offset reduced revenue from state and federal tax cuts.

“So, from the Democratic standpoint, even though it was kind of a wavelet, not a big wave, these moves forward for the Democrats will help increase their powers,” Burkhart said.

#7671. Border wall decision caps busy Monday at SCOTUS

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

It was a busy Monday at the Supreme Court: the justices heard two oral arguments, released an order list, and decided the border wall dispute on the interim docket. Keep reading to catch up on these and other developments.

On Monday, the Supreme Court granted the Trump administration’s request to be allowed to resume construction of its border wall in the Big Bend region of southwestern Texas. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson indicated, without explanation, that she would deny the request. Learn more about the dispute in the On Site section below.

Earlier on Monday, the justices heard arguments in two cases: Nielsen v. Watanabe, on whether and when federal officials can be held liable for constitutional violations; and Hoffmann v. WBI Energy Transmission, Inc., on whether the “just compensation” paid to land owners losing property to a pipeline project should be determined by referring to state law, which often provides for a higher payment than what the Constitution requires.

Also on Monday, the Supreme Court denied review in over 200 cases, including disputes involving the George Floyd protests in Minneapolis, actor Randy Quaid, and the sons of former baseball player Roberto Clemente. It also asked the United States solicitor general to share the government’s views on a case over whether U.S. terrorism victims may sue 21 pharmaceutical and medical-device companies under the Antiterrorism Act for allegedly aiding and abetting Iraqi terrorists. For more on Monday’s order list, see the On Site section.

Today, the justices will hear argument in Department of Labor v. Sun Valley Orchards, LLC, on whether the Constitution allows the executive branch – as opposed to the courts – to adjudicate an employer’s obligation to comply with employment agreements concerning temporary immigrant workers.

On Wednesday, the Supreme Court Building will be closed in recognition of Veterans Day.

Kelsey Dallas is SCOTUSblog's managing editor and the primary author of the SCOTUStoday newsletter.

#7670. Dems ask SEC, DOL to not issue anti-ESG rules: Exclusive

A coalition of 17 blue state finance officials sent a letter to the agencies to counter prior assertions made by their Republican colleagues.

The Democratic finance officials took particular issue with the Republican officials’ letter relying heavily on a federal judge’s ruling against American Airlines in a lawsuit over the management of its retirement plans. The Republican finance officials used U.S. District Court judge Reed O’Connor’s ruling as evidence that the incorporation of factors like ESG is being used to pursue non-pecuniary goals.

The officials included state auditors, treasurers, controllers and comptrollers from New York City, California, Illinois and 12 other states who said that such a characterization of the use of environmental, social and governance factors is “incorrect and dangerously misleading.”

“The decision in Spence v. American Airlines, which dismissed long-term financial interests as a ‘mere pretext,’ fails to reflect the fundamental reality of long-term investing,” the Democratic officials wrote. “Fiduciaries are not speculators — they are stewards of trillions of dollars in assets that must sustain retirees for decades.”

Officials from Connecticut, Colorado, Delaware, Maryland, Massachusetts, Minnesota, Nevada, New Mexico, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont and Washington also signed onto the letter. They said that risks related to climate change, governance failures and systemic issues are “present-day financial realities affecting market valuations, insurance costs, supply chains and infrastructure resilience."

The Republican officials had said in their Jan. 28 letter that they held “serious concerns” that funds were being used to advance ESG or DEI goals and asked for rulemaking to prohibit plans from using assets to “advance political or social goals.” They also asked the Labor Department and SEC to issue comprehensive guidance explicitly saying that making investment decisions or proxy votes based on ESG or diversity, equity and inclusion objectives is “inconsistent with fiduciary duties.”

Connecticut State Treasurer Erick Russell called the request a “dangerous political proposal” in emailed comments to ESG Dive Wednesday, while Illinois State Treasurer Michael Frerichs went a step further, calling the approach “Orwellian” and “a reckless attempt to put politics ahead of sound financial decision-making” in comments Wednesday.

“Forbidding investment managers from assessing real-world risks — whether they stem from supply chain disruptions, environmental instability, shifting consumer demand, or any other factor — would restrict their ability to fully analyze investment opportunities and inherently runs counter to that fiduciary responsibility,” Russell said.

The blue state fiduciaries warned that if utilizing ESG factors in investment decisions was banned for fiduciaries, it could cause weaker investment performance, create greater exposure to market volatility and increase financial vulnerability for retirees.

“As stewards of public funds, we have a responsibility to ensure that our investments provide stable, long-term returns over periods of decades,” Delaware State Treasurer Colleen Davis told ESG Dive. “It is morally reprehensible and financially negligent to play politics with the American people’s retirement savings and investments.”

Acting SEC Chair Mark Uyeda and Acting Labor Secretary Vince Micone are currently in charge of two agencies who are defending a pair of ESG-linked regulations in court. Uyeda said last week he would seek a delay in arguments in lawsuits about the SEC’s climate-risk disclosure rule, indicating the agency as constructed is not inclined to defend the rule. A federal judge recently ruled in favor of the Biden administration’s Labor Department on its regulation allowing fiduciaries to consider ESG and other collateral benefits in the case of a tiebreaker. Experts expect that both rules are endangered under this Trump administration.

#7669. At Paris Peace Forum, Lagarde hails European autonomy as shield against coercion

A digital euro, homegrown AI and whatâs at risk if countries donât establish economic sovereignty â European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde and other leaders called for strategic independence.

PARIS (CN) â On a gray Wednesday morning against the backdrop of the Eiffel Tower, outgoing European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde made her way through a crowded hall, shaking hands as she approached a spotlighted podium.

âSovereignty has traditionally been a legal concept, a state authority over its own territory recognized by others,â she said in her opening speech at the Paris Peace Forum. âAnd it can take the form of defense, capacity to levy tax, capacity to print money â but it’s generally based on a combination of trust and fear.â

Europe’s need for independence has pervaded the continent’s politics since U.S. President Donald Trump took office again, when longstanding alliances entered an era of uncertainty.

Artificial intelligence and new forms of cyber sabotage â like the Oct. 11 attack on French supermarkets that the country has attributed to Iran, which denies involvement â are heightening the urgency to develop self-sufficient systems.

Sovereignty was a central theme at the forum, which gathered hundreds of heads of state, executives and NGOs Tuesday and Wednesday in the Palais de Chaillot. Security was tight; agents asked attendees to take a sip from any drinks in their possession before entering the perimeter.

Lagarde, who announced last month she will step down in February, described how recent shifts in the global geopolitical order have triggered a European reckoning on the risks of economic coercion.

âWe paid a heavy price for depending too much on Russia for our energy, and China has shown that it is willing to restrict export of critical raw materials, rare earths amongst others,â she said. âAnd this summer, even the United States restricted our access to the most advanced artificial intelligence model, [Claude] Mythos.â

She urged the continent to use its roughly 450 million citizens as collective market leverage. She said Europe must develop independent AI innovations for its own security. Europe will also roll out a pilot of a digital euro in 2027 as it works to reconfigure its monetary infrastructure.

âIt’s not a very sexy topic. â¦ It’s nuts and bolts and pipes, but it’s critically important if we’re going to have sovereignty and if we don’t want anybody to suddenly say, âYou know what, I don’t want you to move money on my railroads,’â Lagarde said. âSo we have to build that, and weâre moving fast â¦ years ahead of the U.S., ahead of the Bank of England, ahead of all those other central banks.â

European Parliament member Sandro Gozi warned that autonomy shouldnât be confused with nationalism or isolationism, though far-right agendas often fuse the concepts. Continuing to watch the consequences of Brexit unfold roughly 10 years after the referendum proves his point, he said.

âNationalist forces in Europe and the U.K. talk about independence â¦ but they organize submission,â he said Wednesday. âAny decision which brings you back to 19th century national borders makes you less sovereign, less independent â that was the case with Brexit.â

Lagarde agreed. When the U.K. voted to leave the European Union, she was managing director of the International Monetary Fund, or IMF, and Mark Carney, now prime minister of Canada, was governor of the Bank of England.

âThe two of us, with really solid analysis, with great economists on our side, said â¦ British people will suffer as a result,â she said. âWas our voice heard despite the fact that Mark Carney was the most good-looking central bank governor of the world? That I was the first woman to be managing director of the IMF? No.â

Benjamin Haddad, the French minister delegate for European Affairs, stressed the future of strategic autonomy should be rooted in cooperation.

âI don’t think that you’re stronger and you have more control over your destiny when you isolate yourself from your key friends and partners on all the key issues,â he said. âProsperity, technology, security or tackling illegal migration â you’re stronger when you cooperate closely with your partners and you find common solutions.â

#7667. Smoke flavorings succumb to EU grilling

A food ingredients supplier challenged how regulators assessed its products, but judges found the studies provided did not resolve concerns about DNA damage.

(CN) â A smoky taste is no substitute for proof of safety, an EU court ruled Wednesday, rejecting a bid to greenlight three smoke flavorings.

The General Court of the European Union dismissed Wisconsin- and U.K.-based food ingredients supplier Kerryâs challenge to European Commission decisions refusing to renew the productsâ approvals and removing them from the EUâs authorized list.

Smoke flavorings deliver taste without the smoker. Made from processed wood smoke, they give foods such as cheese, chips and sauces a smoky flavor, including foods that would never traditionally be smoked.

But keeping those products on the market meant showing they were safe, the court held. The responsibility rested with Kerry; regulators did not have to prove that consumers had already been harmed.

The European Food Safety Authority had identified two ingredients shown in oral-exposure tests to damage DNA, the genetic material inside cells. It then estimated how much consumers could get from food. Those amounts exceeded a reference level for low health concerns, and the court found the authority had properly examined exposure as well as the ingredientsâ potential to cause harm.

Kerry argues examining ingredients separately misses what happens when they are mixed together, and that regulators overlooked tests of the finished products. The court found the authority had considered those studies but explained why they did not resolve its concerns.

The court wrote: âIt must be noted that the existence of a scientific debate on the best methodology to be applied is not a sufficient ground to make the methodology used by EFSA in its opinions implausible.â Kerry had not demonstrated sufficient scientific agreement that the authorityâs approach should be abandoned.

Bernd van der Meulen, director and food law specialist at the European Institute for Food Law, found the ruling convincing. He highlighted how deeply the court examined the science despite giving regulators considerable freedom on technical questions. He also welcomed its lack of reference to the precautionary principle â taking protective action when risks remain uncertain â because he considered the scientific findings and Kerryâs responsibility to prove safety sufficient.

Years on the market did not guarantee another approval. EU permissions lasted 10 years, and renewal required safety evidence updated to reflect scientific advances. Kerry applied in June 2022 and supplied more data the following February.

When the authority reassessed eight flavorings in 2023, it identified DNA damage concerns in six and lacked enough information to rule out concerns for the other two. The commission refused renewals in July 2024, giving businesses transition periods to adapt recipes and production.

Natacha Cingotti, campaign strategy lead working on consumer protection at foodwatch international, said the organization had welcomed that precautionary approach. She wanted similar caution applied more often when approving flavorings and additives, arguing that too many substances raising health concerns are still allowed in food.

Kerry also argues restrictions could push manufacturers back toward potentially riskier traditional smoking. The court found the companies had not demonstrated such a shift would happen. Even if it did, that would not justify approving flavorings whose safety had not been established. Transition periods addressed the economic consequences.

Alie de Boer, associate professor in nutrition and food information at Maastricht University, saw a possible missed opportunity to compare the risks of alternatives, though she understood the legal reasoning. She stressed that considering a company’s evidence did not mean accepting its conclusions: The court’s acceptance of EFSA’s assumption that DNA-damaging substances have no safe exposure threshold made scientific uncertainty especially important, while its rejection of Kerry’s alternative method showed how difficult it is to challenge established science without a validated approach.

Luca Knuth, an EU law researcher at Maastricht University and Kiel University, considered the approach defensible, based on public documents and a brief reading of the judgment. He stressed that regulatorsâ scientific freedom still required meaningful court scrutiny. He viewed the responsibility to prove safety as reflecting precaution: Approval could be refused when a company failed to answer credible safety concerns. Choices about handling uncertainty still needed clear, scientifically sound explanations, he said.

The commission defended its position, saying the judgment confirmed the basis for its July 2024 refusal to renew approvals for eight smoke flavorings, including Kerryâs three â SmokEz C-10, SmokEz Enviro-23 and Zesti Smoke Code 10.

Kerry expressed disappointment but stood by the science behind its products. It maintained that extensive data supported their safe use and would review the judgment alongside its concerns about how the flavorings had been assessed.

For customers, however, the companyâs message was to keep preparing for their removal: Existing requirements remained unchanged. âOur focus is on supporting customers through this transition,â Kerry said, reaffirming its commitment to food safety and continued cooperation with regulators.

The court ordered Kerry to pay its own costs and the commissionâs. The company can appeal to the Court of Justice within two months and 10 days of notification, but only on legal grounds. The refusals remain in place, with transition arrangements allowing Kerryâs three primary flavoring products to be placed on the market until July 1, 2029.

Courthouse News reporter Eunseo Hong is based in the Netherlands.

#7663. Justices dubious of fee award in eminent domain dispute about interstate pipeline

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

The argument yesterday in Hoffmann v. WBI Energy Transmission, Inc. left little doubt about how the justices will resolve this one: they seem unlikely to hold that the gas company condemning land for a federally approved pipeline should have to pay attorneys’ fees that the United States would not have to pay if it condemned the land directly.

The dispute involves the 1947 Natural Gas Act’s treatment of interstate natural-gas pipelines. When the federal government approves such a pipeline, the Natural Gas Act allows it to acquire the land in which to build the pipeline or leave that to the gas company. In either case, if the landowner does not agree, a suit exercising the federal government’s right of eminent domain can force a transfer of the land for a “necessary right-of-way,” so long as the landowner receives the “just compensation” that the Fifth Amendment requires when property is “taken for public use.”

The landowners here argue, with some support in the lower courts, that if the pipeline company rather than the United States condemns the land, the pipeline company should be bound by state-law rules that require more compensation than the federal Constitution. In particular, North Dakota law well might require the company to pay the attorneys’ fees of the landowners.

The justices, though, were having none of it. The air was redolent with skepticism from the moment Robert McNamara rose to press the landowners’ view. Justice Clarence Thomas started off by asking – doubtfully – whether “if the U.S. delegates its power … of eminent domain, you’re saying that it brings with it state law trappings of just compensation?” Chief Justice John Roberts quickly interjected that “it seems to me it’s just a more efficient process to have a private developer get the land under the same terms as the federal government without having to pay the attorneys’ fees that the state wants to insist on.” When McNamara stuck to his position, the chief justice eventually concluded the discussion by commenting: “I don’t understand why this isn’t an easy case.”

It seemed for a while that several of the justices would offer a slightly different reason to reject McNamara’s argument, with Justice Sonia Sotomayor coming in quickly to press the idea that “you’re trying to separate the right to eminent domain from the right to compensation, correct?” and then pointing to “a[n] 1893 case … in which we said, [it is] a settled principle of universal law that [they are] inseparably connected. … I don’t see how your separation of these principles honors that.”

For Ketanji Brown Jackson, the problem was McNamara’s assumption “that state law, with respect to just compensation is the default,” and that “it needed to be ousted by congressional expression.” But if that were true, she pointed out, why would Congress have thought it important, in a 1946 condemnation statute adopted just one year before the Natural Gas Act, to take the trouble explicitly to import state law? That statute’s treatment of the condemnation problem appears to contrast sharply with the treatment in the Natural Gas Act just one year later. As Jackson asked pointedly: “What is [that language] doing there if … silence [by Congress means that] state law applies?” Justices Brett Kavanaugh and Amy Coney Barrett pressed McNamara on the same point: they took it as self-evident that the 1946 statute importing state law suggested that a 1947 statute silent on the topic calls for the application of the baseline federal rule emphasized by Thomas and Roberts.

You have to expect it will be pretty hard to fashion a majority if Justice Thomas and the chief justice on one side see it as an “easy case” against you and Jackson and Sotomayor on the other side are predisposed to reject what you have to say. And nothing in the remainder of the argument suggested any reason to think otherwise. The presentations of Paul Hughes (for the pipeline company) and Zoe Jacoby (for the government) were filled for the most part with softball questions speculating about why lower courts might have found such an obvious question challenging.

I would not be at all surprised if this was one of the very first decisions from the November session. The share of simple unanimous statutory cases is not so high as it used to be, but this has all the earmarks of a straightforward unanimous affirmance.

Ronald Mann is a professor of law at Columbia, where he teaches courses in commercial finance, payment systems and deals.

By COLLEEN BARRY Associated Press. Pan Pylas in London, Trisha Thomas and Giulia Arbarello in Rome contributed.

#7660. Trump administration brings White House ballroom battle back to Supreme Court

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

The Trump administration returned to the Supreme Court last week, once again asking the justices to intervene in its ongoing efforts to build a new White House ballroom. On Aug. 31, a divided court paused a ruling by a federal judge in Washington, D.C., that would have halted above-ground construction on the project. In a petition filed on Nov. 5, U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer asked the court to reverse the lower court’s ruling outright or to take up the case and hear oral arguments on the merits. He told the justices that their earlier ruling “has all but answered the question presented” by the dispute, and that the project “should be permitted to move forward outside the shadow of judicial superintendence.”

Construction on the project began in October of last year with the demolition of the East Wing. In December, the National Trust for Historic Preservation – a private nonprofit that describes itself as having “led the movement to save America’s historic places” “[f]or more than 75 years” – filed a lawsuit in federal court, seeking to block the construction until the National Capital Planning Commission and the Commission of Fine Arts could review the plans for the construction; the NCPC could approve those plans; and Congress could authorize the construction.

To support its argument that it had a legal right to sue, known as standing, the trust submitted a declaration from Alison Hoagland, a member who lives in Washington, D.C., and said that she visits the area where the White House is located approximately once per month. Hoagland, who has “expertise in historic architecture,” claimed that the project caused “‘injuries’ to her ‘aesthetic, cultural, and historical interests’ because she finds the ‘scale,’ ‘height,’ and ‘massing’ of the government’s design distasteful.”

Senior U.S. District Judge Leon issued an order in late March that temporarily barred the construction of the ballroom above ground but allowed underground construction – of, for example, bomb shelters and bunkers – to move forward, along with any above-ground construction necessary for safety and security.

Before Leon’s ruling could go into effect, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit froze it to give that court time to consider the government’s appeal. In August, a divided three-judge panel of the D.C. Circuit upheld Leon’s ruling but delayed its effective date for 14 days to allow the federal government to go to the Supreme Court.

Writing for the majority, Judges Patricia Millett and Bradley Garcia emphasized that Congress, and only Congress, has the power “to regulate the construction and demolition of White House structures,” but it has not approved any money for the ballroom construction.

In her dissent, Judge Neomi Rao contended (among other things) that the trust did not have a legal right to bring a lawsuit, known as standing, to try to stop the ballroom construction.

Calling Leon’s ruling “extraordinary and unlawful,” the Trump administration came to the court on its interim docket on Aug. 13. Sauer asked the justices to temporarily pause Leon’s ruling, telling them that it would “halt the ongoing construction of the integrated military complex, including a totally secure ballroom space, at the East Wing of the White House, which is vitally required by national security.” He argued that the trust lacks standing to sue, because its claims rest on a member’s “dislike” for the new construction – which, it said, is not the kind of injury that would allow the lawsuit to go forward.

On Aug. 21, the day that Leon’s order was scheduled to go into effect, Chief Justice John Roberts issued an administrative stay – that is, an order that kept Leon’s order on hold (and permitted construction to continue) – to give the justices additional time to consider the government’s request.

By a vote of 5-4, the court on Aug. 31 granted the government’s application and continued the pause on Leon’s order. In an eight-page, unsigned opinion, the majority stressed that it was not deciding whether the project was legal. Instead, it said, the trust likely lacks standing to challenge the project at all. The harms that Hoagland alleges, the majority wrote, are not the kind of “concrete” and specific injuries required to bring a lawsuit. Moreover, the majority said, if Leon’s order were allowed to go into effect, the government would be permanently harmed – another key criterion in determining whether to grant emergency relief. Among other things, it noted, senior government officials “attest[] that constructing something approximating the height and mass of the intended above-ground ballroom is ‘crucial’ to the security of the below-ground military installation.”

Roberts dissented, in an opinion joined by Justices Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan, and Ketanji Brown Jackson. In his view, the construction “is likely unlawful,” and the majority’s decision was “no victory for the separation of powers.” He contended that the trust did have standing to sue because “[a] historic preservationist such as Hoagland can be aesthetically injured in a concrete, particularized way by the transformation of a historic building that she frequently enjoys, just as,” based on prior court precedent, “an environmentalist can sustain a concrete, particularized aesthetic injury from the extinction of a particular animal or the transformation of a particular forest or river that he regularly enjoys.”

In its Nov. 5 petition, the Trump administration argued that “the East Wing renovation is a vital national-security effort taking place on the White House grounds with the President’s personal involvement,” and that it has “proceeded swiftly since construction began in October 2025, in keeping with the urgency of remedying the East Wing’s obsolete and vulnerable security infrastructure, all as this President faces an onslaught of assassination attempts.” Because Leon’s order blocked the project “at the behest of a single passerby who complains that she expects to dislike its ultimate design,” Sauer wrote, his “decision is demonstrably flawed.”

Sauer acknowledged that the court’s Aug. 31 ruling came on the interim docket and therefore “only involve[d] a preliminary look at the merits and equities” of the dispute. But, he continued, in this case “[t]here is nothing further or new that this Court needs to decide after its” earlier opinion “in order to answer the question presented” by the government’s new filing – specifically, whether Leon was wrong to block “the ongoing renovation of the East Wing of the White House.” This is especially true, Sauer suggested, given the court made its Aug. 31 decision “after extensive briefing, and issue[d] detailed majority and dissenting opinions addressing” the issues in the case.

Sauer urged the court to summarily reverse Leon’s decision – that is, to reverse it without additional briefing or oral argument – or, at a minimum, grant review and hear oral arguments.

The trust’s response to the government’s petition is currently due on Dec. 7.
